## Notes on Lamentations 2 (traditional readings)

**Whole chapter (vv. 1–9)**
- Matthew Henry says the main stress of these verses is on God's own hand in Judah's troubles. Once God was the friend of His church; now He acts toward her like an enemy. Henry adds that this is different from God actually hating her. People can be very angry with those they love without being their enemies. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_002.cfm
- The Expositor's Bible says the poet keeps repeating that God is acting as an opponent. God isn't just letting Israel's enemies do damage; God is doing it Himself. The poet says nothing about Nebuchadnezzar, whom he treats as only a tool of the real Enemy. The commentator warns that preaching which skips over this hard side of God fails to stir consciences. It also makes the gospel of redemption meaningless, because people can't value rescue from a danger they don't see. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/lamentations/2.htm

**v. 1:** Guzik notes that Jerusalem once knew the cloud of God's glory (1 Kings 8). Ezekiel saw that cloud leave the city under judgment (Ezek. 10). Now the cloud that covers Zion is a cloud of anger. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/

**v. 2:**
- Guzik says these verses begin a long list of "He has" statements. The point is that the destruction comes from God, even though the Babylonian army carried it out. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/
- He also says titles like "Daughter of Zion" and "Daughter of Judah" are privileges that carry duties. Israel thought only of the privilege and forgot the duty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/
- The Bible Hub summary (chapter overview) uses this verse to show that God's anger here is personal, not blind fate. It ties the verse to the urgency of seeking God's mercy. https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/lamentations/2.htm

**v. 3:** Henry asks what Israel's right hand could do once God pulled it back and withered it, as He did Jeroboam's. A people known for courage could no longer hold their ground. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_002.cfm

**v. 4:** Guzik says God's skill and strength ("His right hand") were turned against Jerusalem. He quotes Ryken: the usual Old Testament picture of God as a warrior fighting for His people is reversed here, and God fights against them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/

**v. 5:** Henry says God swallowed up even the palaces of princes, however grand and well guarded. When God's judgments come, palaces fall as easily as cottages. With their defences gone, the people's mourning naturally grew. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_002.cfm

**v. 6:** Guzik says that when the temple and city were destroyed, the festivals and Sabbaths tied to them stopped as well. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/

**v. 7:**
- Guzik lists the losses: God rejected His altar and abandoned His sanctuary. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/
- Henry says that once the walls of the palaces were handed to the enemy, the palaces themselves were soon broken into. Walls can't protect a city unless God Himself is its "wall of fire." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_002.cfm
- The Bible Hub summary raises a study question here: if God left His altar, how does that fit with His presence being everlasting? The extract doesn't answer it. https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/lamentations/2.htm

**v. 8:**
- Guzik says Jerusalem's wall was its security; once it fell, anyone could take the city. "Stretched out a line" pictures careful measuring, the way a builder works, so nothing was accidental. He also sees v. 8 ("determined to destroy") and v. 17 ("done what He planned") as a frame around the chapter: the judgment announced is the judgment carried out. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/
- Henry also says God acted in anger but deliberately, by an earlier purpose: He brought in the Chaldean army on purpose. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_002.cfm

**v. 9:** The Expositor's Bible discusses "the law is no more." The Authorised and Revised Versions link the phrase with "among the nations," as though the exiled king lived where the Torah wasn't kept. The commentator prefers to read it with the surrounding lines: with the rulers removed, Jews at home lost the running of their law. He says good government is a real blessing that people in peaceful times take for granted. He also ties the loss of rulers to the silence of prophecy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/lamentations/2.htm

**v. 10:** Guzik quotes Ellison: mentioning "elders" and "young women" probably means the whole surviving population. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/

**v. 11:**
- Guzik says Jeremiah's tears, inner turmoil and even sickness show his deep compassion. He quotes Poole: the vivid bodily language simply expresses very great grief. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/
- He also quotes Harrison: the fainting children contrast with the promise of children playing in Jerusalem's streets after restoration (Zech. 8:5). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/

**vv. 11–12 (children suffering):** The Expositor's Bible asks why innocent children suffer for evils they didn't cause. It answers in three steps:
- The blame belongs to the stubborn leaders who ignored the prophets' warnings, not to God.
- People are bound together, and on the whole that bond helps children more than it harms them.
- Even so, the riddle isn't fully solved, and we have a duty to relieve such suffering.

https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/lamentations/2.htm

**v. 13:** Guzik says Jeremiah, who often spoke of Jerusalem having no comforter, now can't comfort her himself, because the ruin is too wide to help. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/

**v. 14:**
- Guzik says Judah's last days were full of false prophets who promised rescue from Babylon and a quick return of the captives. Because they never exposed the people's sin, no comfort was possible. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/
- The Bible Hub summary uses this verse to stress the failure of prophets and leaders to point out sin. https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/lamentations/2.htm

**v. 17:**
- Guzik says this fulfils the purpose announced in v. 8. Had Jerusalem stayed faithful, no enemy could have conquered her. Her persistent sin is why God raised up her enemies' "horn" (strength). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/
- The Bible Hub summary reads the verse as showing God's control: His plans are always fulfilled. https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/lamentations/2.htm

**v. 18:** Guzik reads "let your tears run down like a river" as a taunt by the gloating enemies, who want Jerusalem to weep forever. In the extract I saw, no other source reads it this way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/

**v. 19:** The Bible Hub summary takes the call to cry out in the night as a sign that God is near and ready to listen even in the darkest times. https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/lamentations/2.htm

**v. 20:**
- Guzik reads this as Jerusalem's agonised plea for God to look at the city He loved. She points to the depth of her suffering: mothers eating their children, and priests and prophets killed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/
- The Bible Hub summary lists the cannibalism reference as a hard question for study. The extract doesn't answer it. https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/lamentations/2.htm

**v. 21:**
- Henry says no age was spared. Young boys too young to fight and old men past fighting died by the sword and lay in the streets unburied. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_002.cfm
- Guzik says Jerusalem, speaking as a person, knows this was God's deserved judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/

**v. 22:** Guzik says it was the LORD who "invited" the terrors that surrounded Jerusalem. The enemy destroyed everyone the city had raised. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-2/
